terminus.finding: Shiue Fang-Jye and Pan Kuan-Chih (2009) argue that aging-in-place support should not be concentrated only in a community activity center: additional stopping points improve accessibility and social interaction, and community care works by linking formal and informal resources while keeping people in familiar environments.
terminus.generated: DISTRIBUTED-SUPPORT-NODE MODEL: lowering a barrier need not mean erasing the habitat or centralizing provision. A system can preserve familiar relational territory while adding multiple low-intensity support nodes. This is a concrete counterexample to a simplistic friction-versus-access tradeoff: access can increase by distributing interfaces through an existing ecology rather than replacing that ecology.

quality.evidence: literature review + interviews/data analysis as reported

terminus.relationToPrevious: Refines FRICTION-AS-HABITAT. The choice is not only keep friction versus remove friction. A third design is to leave the habitat substantially intact while inserting distributed support points that reduce specific access costs.
terminus.next: seek a non-care domain where distributed interfaces reduce access costs without dissolving the host ecology; if it repeats, promote this from case-specific synthesis to reusable design principle
